title: This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel
gist: Hertha Metals founder Laureen Meroueh built a single-step furnace that swaps coal for natural gas to cut steelmaking emissions by at least half and costs by 25%, deliberately staying fossil-fuel-based for now rather than betting on hydrogen, and has scaled from one ton of steel per day toward a 500,000-ton/year roadmap on only about $20 million raised.

insights.claim: Conventional steelmaking, largely unchanged in process since the 1850s, melts iron ore in coal-fired blast furnaces at very high temperatures to strip out oxygen, and generates roughly 7% of global carbon emissions that drive climate change — comparable to the fashion industry's footprint.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Sizes steel as a top-tier decarbonization target on par with an entire other major polluting industry, framing the addressable emissions opportunity for any credible steel-decarbonization technology.
insights.locator: The process relies on coal, and it generates roughly 7%

insights.claim: Decarbonizing steel has proved difficult because profit margins in the industry are tight and blast furnaces have very long service lives, making it hard to justify the capital investment needed to replace existing infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Explains the structural investment barrier that any green-steel technology must overcome — it must compete on cost, not just emissions, given thin margins and sunk capital in existing furnaces.

insights.claim: Hertha Metals founder Laureen Meroueh invented a furnace that turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step (versus multiple steps in conventional processing) and substitutes natural gas for coal, which she says cuts emissions by at least half and costs by 25% compared with standard steelmaking.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified cost-and-emissions improvement claim (half the emissions, 25% lower cost) that is the core investable thesis for the company, pending third-party verification at scale.
insights.locator: Her method turns iron ore into refined liquid steel

insights.claim: Unlike competing green-steel approaches that use hydrogen to free oxygen from iron ore and could eventually eliminate emissions entirely, Hertha deliberately continues relying on fossil fuels (natural gas) for now to keep costs down, while designing the plant so it could switch to a fully decarbonized system without major hardware changes if hydrogen becomes more affordable.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A deliberate near-term-pragmatism-over-purity strategy: Hertha bets that incremental, cost-competitive decarbonization beats waiting for a zero-carbon hydrogen system that isn't yet economical, a framework applicable to other hard-to-abate industrial sectors.
insights.locator: Meroueh says Hertha is content for the time being

insights.claim: A director at the National Fuel Cell Research Center says there is huge value in shrinking the size of steel production systems, because conventional blast furnaces are massive, inefficient, and energy-intensive, so even modest energy-efficiency gains represent a significant step forward.
insights.speaker: Iryna Zenyuk, via Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: An independent academic validating the directional value of Hertha's system-simplification approach, distinct from Meroueh's own claims.
insights.quote: There's huge value in reducing the size of this production system.
insights.locator: If it catches on, the tech could be transformative

insights.claim: Hertha's pilot plant in Conroe, Texas currently produces one metric ton of steel per day; a new adjacent plant is planned to produce 10,000 metric tons of high-purity steel per year and reach full capacity by the end of 2027; Meroueh projects scaling to 500,000 metric tons per year by 2030 with the addition of a third site.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, time-stamped production scale-up roadmap (1 ton/day now to 500,000 tons/year by 2030) against which to track execution risk and progress.
insights.locator: That facility can produce one metric ton of steel per day

insights.claim: Hertha's projected 500,000-metric-ton annual output by 2030 would still be only a small fraction of the roughly 80 million metric tons of steel produced annually in the US, though an academic reviewer notes that even producing one metric ton is itself an achievement for a new steelmaking process.
insights.speaker: Iryna Zenyuk, via Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Frames the realistic near-term addressable share of the US steel market (well under 1%), useful for tempering expectations about near-term market impact even if the technology succeeds.
insights.locator: That's only a fraction of the approximately 80 million metric tons

insights.claim: A Khosla Ventures partner and Hertha investor says the company's scale-up is impressive given how little it has spent, noting that competitors have produced far less steel despite raising $50 million to $100 million, while Hertha had raised only about $20 million in funding as of July 2026.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan, via Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A capital-efficiency comparison against unnamed competitors, positioning Hertha as potentially raising less dilutive capital for equivalent or greater output than better-funded green-steel rivals.
insights.locator: Competitors, he notes, have created far less steel
